justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a mild upward drift from what I assessed as the current price level around $132–133. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price, assuming mean-reverting intraday dynamics with minimal net movement — essentially expecting the asset to close near where it opened with only slight momentum carrying it marginally higher. At the one-week horizon, I applied a small positive drift assumption, reflecting either a modest bullish bias in recent price action or a slight risk premium built into the forward expectation. At the one-month horizon, the estimate of $134 continues that gentle upward trajectory, consistent with a low-volatility drift assumption rather than any strong directional conviction.

The confidence interval widths widen appropriately as the horizon extends, reflecting the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans just six points, implying relatively low realized volatility expectations — consistent with an asset trading in a calm regime without imminent catalysts. By one week, the interval expands to twelve points, and by one month it reaches twenty-four points, roughly doubling at each step. This scaling is broadly consistent with volatility growing proportionally to the square root of time, suggesting I was implicitly assuming an annualized volatility somewhere in the range of 15–20%, which is moderate but not unusual for many financial instruments.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst — such as a strong earnings release, favorable macroeconomic data, or a shift in central bank policy signaling — could drive a sharp rally that breaks above the upper bounds. On the downside, a risk-off episode triggered by geopolitical events, credit stress, or a broad equity selloff could push prices well below the lower bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon where tail risks have more time to materialize.

It is also worth noting that these intervals assume a relatively stationary volatility environment. If volatility regimes shift — for instance, if implied volatility spikes due to an unexpected macro shock — the actual distribution of outcomes could be considerably fatter-tailed than my intervals suggest. Liquidity events, forced institutional selling, or correlated asset dislocations could all produce outcomes in the 5–10% range beyond my stated bounds, which by construction my 90% confidence interval explicitly leaves 10% probability mass to cover.
